claim: Studies in a variety of species have shown evidence for positively selected variants introduced into a population via introgression from another, distantly related population.
source: Studies in a variety of species have shown evidence for positively selected variants introduced into a population via introgression from another, distantly related population—a process known as adaptive introgression.
evidence: This is a general statement about findings in the literature, supported by the context of the manuscript.

claim: The CNN architecture exhibits 95% accuracy on simulated data, even when the genomes are unphased.
source: Our CNN architecture exhibits 95% accuracy on simulated data, even when the genomes are unphased, and accuracy decreases only moderately in the presence of heterosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results of the CNN performance evaluation on simulated datasets as described in the Results section.

claim: Accuracy decreases only moderately in the presence of heterosis.
source: Our CNN architecture exhibits 95% accuracy on simulated data, even when the genomes are unphased, and accuracy decreases only moderately in the presence of heterosis.
evidence: This is based on simulations incorporating a distribution of fitness effects with recessive dominance.

claim: Human evolution during the Pleistocene was characterised by numerous episodes of interbreeding between distantly related groups.
source: Ancient DNA studies have shown that human evolution during the Pleistocene was characterised by numerous episodes of interbreeding between distantly related groups (Green et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2010; Meyer et al., 2012; Prüfer et al., 2017; Kuhlwilm et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to ancient DNA studies.

claim: Considerable portions of the modern human gene pool derive from Neanderthals and Denisovans.
source: We now know, for example, that considerable portions of the modern human gene pool derive from Neanderthals and Denisovans (Green et al., 2010; Reich et al., 2010; Prüfer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on Neanderthal and Denisovan admixture.

claim: A large proportion of Neanderthal ancestry was likely negatively selected.
source: While recent evidence suggests that a large proportion of Neanderthal ancestry was likely negatively selected (Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Juric et al., 2016), there is also support for positive selection on a smaller proportion of the genome—a phenomenon known as adaptive introgression (AI) (Whitney et al., 2006; Hawks and Cochran, 2006; Racimo et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on selection against Neanderthal ancestry.

claim: There is support for positive selection on a smaller proportion of the genome, a phenomenon known as adaptive introgression.
source: While recent evidence suggests that a large proportion of Neanderthal ancestry was likely negatively selected (Harris and Nielsen, 2016; Juric et al., 2016), there is also support for positive selection on a smaller proportion of the genome—a phenomenon known as adaptive introgression (AI) (Whitney et al., 2006; Hawks and Cochran, 2006; Racimo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression.

claim: Genomic evidence for adaptive introgression has been found in butterflies.
source: Genomic evidence for AI has been found in numerous other species, including butterflies (Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017), mosquitoes (Norris et al., 2015), hares (Jones et al., 2018), poplars (Suarez-Gonzalez et al., 2016), and monkeyflowers (Hendrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression in butterflies.

claim: Genomic evidence for adaptive introgression has been found in mosquitoes.
source: Genomic evidence for AI has been found in numerous other species, including butterflies (Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017), mosquitoes (Norris et al., 2015), hares (Jones et al., 2018), poplars (Suarez-Gonzalez et al., 2016), and monkeyflowers (Hendrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression in mosquitoes.

claim: Genomic evidence for adaptive introgression has been found in hares.
source: Genomic evidence for AI has been found in numerous other species, including butterflies (Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017), mosquitoes (Norris et al., 2015), hares (Jones et al., 2018), poplars (Suarez-Gonzalez et al., 2016), and monkeyflowers (Hendrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression in hares.

claim: Genomic evidence for adaptive introgression has been found in poplars.
source: Genomic evidence for AI has been found in numerous other species, including butterflies (Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017), mosquitoes (Norris et al., 2015), hares (Jones et al., 2018), poplars (Suarez-Gonzalez et al., 2016), and monkeyflowers (Hendrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression in poplars.

claim: Genomic evidence for adaptive introgression has been found in monkeyflowers.
source: Genomic evidence for AI has been found in numerous other species, including butterflies (Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017), mosquitoes (Norris et al., 2015), hares (Jones et al., 2018), poplars (Suarez-Gonzalez et al., 2016), and monkeyflowers (Hendrick et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on adaptive introgression in monkeyflowers.

claim: A variant of the gene EPAS1 has been shown to have introgressed from an archaic human population into the ancestors of Tibetans.
source: For example, a variant of the gene EPAS1 has been shown to have introgressed from an archaic human population into the ancestors of Tibetans, and subsequently risen in frequency in the latter population, as a consequence of positive selection to high altitude (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on EPAS1 introgression in Tibetans.

claim: The EPAS1 variant subsequently rose in frequency in Tibetans as a consequence of positive selection to high altitude.
source: For example, a variant of the gene EPAS1 has been shown to have introgressed from an archaic human population into the ancestors of Tibetans, and subsequently risen in frequency in the latter population, as a consequence of positive selection to high altitude (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on EPAS1 introgression in Tibetans.

claim: A different high-frequency EPAS1 variant is uniquely found in Tibetan Mastiffs and appears to have introgressed via admixture with Tibetan wolves.
source: A different high-frequency EPAS1 variant is also uniquely found in Tibetan Mastiffs, and appears to also have introgressed into this gene pool via admixture with a different species, in this case Tibetan wolves (Miao et al., 2017), likely due to the same selective pressures.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on EPAS1 introgression in Tibetan Mastiffs.

claim: Deep learning techniques are increasingly becoming a popular solution to address problems in population genetics.
source: To overcome the need to compress data into summary statistics (which might miss important features), deep learning techniques are increasingly becoming a popular solution to address problems in population genetics.
evidence: This is supported by the context and citations to deep learning applications in population genetics.

claim: Deep learning has been applied to inference of demographic histories.
source: These problems include the inference of demographic histories (Sheehan and Song, 2016; Flagel et al., 2019; Villanea and Schraiber, 2019; Mondal et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021), admixture (Blischak et al., 2021), recombination (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Adrion et al., 2020b), and natural selection (Schrider and Kern, 2018; Sheehan and Song, 2016; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using deep learning for demographic inference.

claim: Deep learning has been applied to inference of admixture.
source: These problems include the inference of demographic histories (Sheehan and Song, 2016; Flagel et al., 2019; Villanea and Schraiber, 2019; Mondal et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021), admixture (Blischak et al., 2021), recombination (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Adrion et al., 2020b), and natural selection (Schrider and Kern, 2018; Sheehan and Song, 2016; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study using deep learning for admixture inference.

claim: Deep learning has been applied to inference of recombination.
source: These problems include the inference of demographic histories (Sheehan and Song, 2016; Flagel et al., 2019; Villanea and Schraiber, 2019; Mondal et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021), admixture (Blischak et al., 2021), recombination (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Adrion et al., 2020b), and natural selection (Schrider and Kern, 2018; Sheehan and Song, 2016; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using deep learning for recombination inference.

claim: Deep learning has been applied to inference of natural selection.
source: These problems include the inference of demographic histories (Sheehan and Song, 2016; Flagel et al., 2019; Villanea and Schraiber, 2019; Mondal et al., 2019; Sanchez et al., 2021), admixture (Blischak et al., 2021), recombination (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Adrion et al., 2020b), and natural selection (Schrider and Kern, 2018; Sheehan and Song, 2016; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using deep learning for selection inference.

claim: Convolutional neural networks are a family of methods originally designed for image recognition and segmentation.
source: Among the techniques in this field, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a family of methods originally designed for image recognition and segmentation (LeCun and Bengio, 1995; Krizhevsky et al., 2012), which have been recently applied to population genetic data (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021; Blischak et al., 2021; Sanchez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational CNN papers.

claim: CNNs have been recently applied to population genetic data.
source: Among the techniques in this field, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a family of methods originally designed for image recognition and segmentation (LeCun and Bengio, 1995; Krizhevsky et al., 2012), which have been recently applied to population genetic data (Chan et al., 2018; Flagel et al., 2019; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021; Blischak et al., 2021; Sanchez et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies applying CNNs to population genetics.

claim: No dedicated attempts have been made to identify adaptive introgression from population genomic data using deep learning.
source: Despite the recent advances in deep learning for population genetics, no dedicated attempts have been made to identify AI from population genomic data.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claim: The method has >88% precision to detect adaptive introgression.
source: The method has >88% precision to detect AI and is effective on both ancient and recently selected introgressed haplotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the performance evaluation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The method is effective on both ancient and recently selected introgressed haplotypes.
source: The method has >88% precision to detect AI and is effective on both ancient and recently selected introgressed haplotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the performance evaluation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The method was applied to human genomic datasets to detect candidates for adaptive introgression.
source: We then applied our method to population genomic datasets where the donor population is either Neanderthals or Denisovans and the recipient populations are Europeans or Melanesians, respectively.
evidence: This is described in the Results section and supported by the data analysis.

claim: When training a CNN on Demographic Model A1 using phased data, a precision of 90.2% and 97.9% negative predictive value were obtained.
source: When training a CNN on Demographic Model A1 using phased data, we obtained a precision of 90.2% (the proportion of AI predictions that were AI simulations) and 97.9% negative predictive value (NPV; the proportion of 'not-AI' predictions that were either neutral or sweep simulations) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The network output higher probabilities for AI simulations with larger selection coefficients.
source: The network output higher probabilities for AI simulations with larger selection coefficients, and for older times of onset of selection.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of CNN predictions across different parameter values.

claim: The network output higher probabilities for AI simulations with older times of onset of selection.
source: The network output higher probabilities for AI simulations with larger selection coefficients, and for older times of onset of selection.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of CNN predictions across different parameter values.

claim: The network falsely classified neutral simulations as AI more frequently than it falsely classified sweep simulations.
source: We also observed that the network falsely classified neutral simulations as AI more frequently than it falsely classified sweep simulations.
evidence: This is supported by the confusion matrix and performance analysis.

claim: When the CNN was trained on Demographic Model A1 assuming genotypes were unphased, the results were very similar, with 88.1% precision and 98.7% NPV.
source: When the CNN was trained on this same demographic model assuming genotypes were unphased, the results were very similar, with 88.1% precision and 98.7% NPV.
evidence: This is supported by the performance evaluation on unphased data.

claim: When training a CNN on Demographic Model B, 88.8% precision and 82.5% NPV were obtained.
source: When training a CNN on Demographic Model B (assuming unphased genotypes, as accurately phased data are not readily available for Melanesian genomes), we obtained 88.8% precision and 82.5% NPV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The network had greater precision when detecting AI derived from the more ancient pulse of Denisovan gene flow than the younger pulse.
source: We note here that the network had greater precision when detecting AI derived from the more ancient pulse of Denisovan gene flow than the younger pulse.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of CNN performance on simulations with two pulses of gene flow.

claim: Heterosis following introgression only slightly increases the false positive rate.
source: To assess whether heterosis following introgression affects the false positive rates in our CNN, we simulated a distribution of fitness effects (DFE) with recessive dominance for 70% of derived mutations (the rest were simulated as neutral), and found this only slightly increases the false positive rate (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by simulations incorporating a DFE and the results shown in Figure 2.

claim: VolcanoFinder performed poorly for the demographic models considered in this study.
source: VolcanoFinder performed poorly for the demographic models considered here—in some cases, worse than guessing randomly.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The CNN is closest to a perfect MCC-F1 score for Demographic model A1 and B, closely followed by the Q95(1%, 100%) statistic.
source: Our CNN is closest to a perfect MCC-F1 score for Demographic model A1 and B, closely followed by the Q95(1%, 100%) and then U(1%, 20%, 100%) statistics developed in Racimo et al., 2017b.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Weak demographic misspecification resulted in only a small performance reduction.
source: We considered weak misspecification, where the true demographic history is similar to Demographic Model A1 but also includes archaic admixture within Africa following Ragsdale and Gravel, 2019 (Demographic Model A2; Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This resulted in only a small performance reduction.
evidence: This is supported by the misspecification analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under strong demographic misspecification, the performance of the CNN was noticeably worse than that of the summary statistics.
source: We also considered strong misspecification, where the true demographic history is Demographic Model B. As there are more Melanesian individuals than European individuals in our simulations (because we aimed to mimic the real number of genomes available in our data analysis below), we downsampled the Melanesian genomes to match the number of European genomes, so as to perform a fair misspecification comparison. In this case, the performance of the CNN was noticeably worse than that of the summary statistics, but still better than VolcanoFinder.
evidence: This is supported by the misspecification analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Q95(1%, 100%) statistic was the most robust method for both cases of misspecification.
source: Interestingly, we found that the Q95(1%, 100%) statistic was the most robust method for both cases of misspecification.
evidence: This is supported by the misspecification analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: When the network was presented with an AI matrix, it focused most of the attention on the Neanderthal and European haplotypes, rather than on the African haplotypes.
source: Our results show that when the network was presented with an AI matrix, it focused most of the attention on the Neanderthal and European haplotypes, rather than on the African haplotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the saliency map analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: In non-AI scenarios, the network focused sharply on the Neanderthal and left-most European haplotypes.
source: In non-AI scenarios, the network focused sharply on the Neanderthal and left-most European haplotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the saliency map analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The saliency maps show a concentration of attention in the central region of the genomic window, closer to where the selected mutation was drawn.
source: The saliency maps also show a concentration of attention in the central region of the genomic window, closer to where the selected mutation was drawn (even though this mutation does not exist in neutral simulations, and was removed from sweep and AI simulations before constructing genotype matrices; see Methods).
evidence: This is supported by the saliency map analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Several candidate genes for Neanderthal AI in Europeans have been reported before, including BNC2, KCNQ2/EEF1A2, WRD88/GPATCH1 and TANC1.
source: We found several candidate genes for AI that have been reported before (Sankararaman et al., 2014; Vernot and Akey, 2014; Gittelman et al., 2016; Racimo et al., 2017b), including BNC2, KCNQ2/EEF1A2 WRD88/GPATCH1 and TANC1.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to human genomic data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: The candidate region on chromosome 2 around TANC1 extends farther downstream, also overlapping BAZ2B.
source: Notably, the candidate region we identify on chromosome 2 around TANC1 extends farther downstream of this gene, also overlapping BAZ2B (Appendix 4—figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of candidate regions shown in Appendix 4—figure 3.

claim: BAZ2B codes for a protein related to chromatin remodelling, and may have a role in transcriptional activation.
source: This codes for a protein related to chromatin remodelling, and may have a role in transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is a statement about the function of BAZ2B based on biological knowledge.

claim: Mutations in BAZ2B have recently been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability.
source: Mutations in BAZ2B have recently been associated with neurodevelopmental disorders, including developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability (Scott et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on BAZ2B mutations.

claim: Two novel candidates for Neanderthal AI were found spanning the regions chr6:28.18 Mb–28.32 Mb and chr20:62.1 Mb–62.28 Mb, including multiple genes encoding zinc finger proteins.
source: Additionally, we found two novel candidates for AI that have not been previously reported, spanning the regions chr6:28.18 Mb–28.32 Mb (Appendix 4—figure 7) and chr20:62.1 Mb–62.28 Mb (Appendix 4—figure 13), including multiple genes encoding zinc finger proteins.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to human genomic data.

claim: Among the top candidates for Denisovan AI in Melanesians is TNFAIP3, which has been reported before.
source: Among the top candidates, we found a previously reported candidate for AI in Melanesians: TNFAIP3 (Vernot et al., 2016; Gittelman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Denisovan substitutions carried by the introgressed haplotype in TNFAIP3 have been found to enhance the immune response by tuning the phosphorylation of the encoded A20 protein.
source: Denisovan substitutions carried by the introgressed haplotype in this gene have been found to enhance the immune response by tuning the phosphorylation of the encoded A20 protein, which is an immune response inhibitor (Zammit et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on TNFAIP3 function.

claim: Evidence for Denisovan AI in Melanesians was found at a region overlapping the CYCS gene.
source: One of the regions with strong evidence for AI (chr7:25.1 Mb–25.2 Mb; Appendix 5—figure 8) overlaps the CYCS gene.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data.

claim: CYCS codes for cytochrome C, a small heme protein that plays a crucial role in the electron transport chain in mitochondria.
source: This gene codes for cytochrome C: a small heme protein that plays a crucial role in the electron transport chain in mitochondria, and has been associated with various blood-related diseases, like thrombocytopenia (Morison et al., 2008; De Rocco et al., 2014; Uchiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on CYCS function and disease associations.

claim: A top candidate region for Denisovan AI is upstream of PRDM4 and ASCL4.
source: Another top candidate region (chr12:108.24–108.34 Mb, Appendix 5—figure 13) is upstream of PRDM4 and ASCL4.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data.

claim: PRDM4 codes for a transcription factor that may be involved in the nerve growth factor cell survival pathway and might play a role in tumour suppression.
source: The former gene codes for a transcription factor that may be involved in the nerve growth factor cell survival pathway and might play a role in tumour suppression (Yang and Huang, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on PRDM4 function.

claim: ASCL4 codes for a transcription factor that may be involved in skin development.
source: The latter gene codes for a different transcription factor that may be involved in skin development (Jonsson et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on ASCL4 function.

claim: Signatures of Denisovan AI were detected in a region in chromosome 3 near SUMF1 and LRNN1, which was also identified in Jacobs et al., 2019.
source: We detected signatures of Denisovan AI in a region in chromosome 3 near SUMF1 and LRNN1 (Appendix 5—figure 2), which was also identified in Jacobs et al., 2019.
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data and comparison with a previous study.

claim: SUMF1 codes for an enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of sulfate esters, which has been associated with sulfatase deficiency.
source: SUMF1 codes for an enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of sulfate esters, which has been associated with sulfatase deficiency (Cosma et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on SUMF1 function.

claim: LRNN1 encodes a protein involved in neuronal differentiation, which has been associated with neuroblastoma and Alzheimer's disease.
source: LRNN1 encodes a protein involved in neuronal differentiation, which has been associated with neuroblastoma and Alzheimer's disease (Bai et al., 2014; Hossain et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on LRNN1 function and disease associations.

claim: A candidate region for Denisovan AI is in chromosome 7 and is upstream of SFRP4.
source: Another candidate region is in chromosome 7 and is upstream of SFRP4 (Appendix 5—figure 9), which encodes a protein associated with diabetes (Mahdi et al., 2012) and Pyle's disease (Kiper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data.

claim: SFRP4 encodes a protein associated with diabetes and Pyle's disease.
source: Another candidate region is in chromosome 7 and is upstream of SFRP4 (Appendix 5—figure 9), which encodes a protein associated with diabetes (Mahdi et al., 2012) and Pyle's disease (Kiper et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on SFRP4 function and disease associations.

claim: There is a candidate region for Denisovan AI upstream of RAB27A, in chromosome 15.
source: Moreover, there is also a candidate region upstream of RAB27A, in chromosome 15 (Appendix 5—figure 18).
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data.

claim: Mutations in RAB27A cause Griscelli syndrome, which results in pigmentary dilution in the hair and skin, as well as melanosome accumulation in melanocytes.
source: Mutations in this gene cause Griscelli syndrome, which results in pigmentary dilution in the hair and skin, as well as melanosome accumulation in melanocytes (Ménasché et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on RAB27A function and disease associations.

claim: Evidence for Denisovan AI was found in two nearby regions in chromosome 14, one overlapping with PRKCH and the other with KCNH5.
source: Finally, we found evidence for Denisovan AI in two nearby regions in chromosome 14 (Appendix 5—figure 15 and Appendix 5—figure 16). One of these overlaps with PRKCH—encoding a protein kinase associated with cerebral infarction (Kubo et al., 2007). The other overlaps with KCNH5—coding for a potassium channel that may be associated with epileptic encephalopathy (Veeramah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the application of the CNN to Melanesian genomic data.

claim: PRKCH encodes a protein kinase associated with cerebral infarction.
source: One of these overlaps with PRKCH—encoding a protein kinase associated with cerebral infarction (Kubo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on PRKCH function and disease associations.

claim: KCNH5 codes for a potassium channel that may be associated with epileptic encephalopathy.
source: The other overlaps with KCNH5—coding for a potassium channel that may be associated with epileptic encephalopathy (Veeramah et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on KCNH5 function and disease associations.

claim: The method has high precision when reporting candidate AI loci, and high negative predictive value when rejecting loci as not-AI, with greater than 90% accuracy under a variety of different selection scenarios.
source: The method has high precision when reporting candidate AI loci, and high negative predictive value when rejecting loci as not-AI: we obtain greater than 90% accuracy under a variety of different selection scenarios (Appendix 2—table 1), with low false positive rates.
evidence: This is supported by the performance evaluation results presented in Appendix 2—table 1.

claim: Heterosis following introgression can inflate false positive detection of AI by the CNN to a small extent.
source: As reported previously (Kim et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020), heterosis following introgression can produce patterns very similar to AI, and we found this can inflate false positive detection of AI by our CNN to a small extent.
evidence: This is supported by simulations incorporating a DFE and comparison with previous studies.

claim: When the demographic model is correctly specified, the CNN performed better than using summary statistics.
source: When the demographic model is correctly specified, our CNN performed better than using summary statistics, although the Q95(1%, 100%) statistic (Racimo et al., 2017b) also performed remarkably well.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Q95(1%, 100%) statistic performed remarkably well.
source: When the demographic model is correctly specified, our CNN performed better than using summary statistics, although the Q95(1%, 100%) statistic (Racimo et al., 2017b) also performed remarkably well.
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of methods shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: An outlier approach based on Q95 may be a better choice than the CNN when there is uncertainty regarding the demographic history of the study system.
source: Because of its relative robustness to model misspecification, an outlier approach based on Q95 may be a better choice than our CNN when there is uncertainty regarding the demographic history of the study system.
evidence: This is based on the misspecification analysis and comparison of methods.

claim: The CNN took approximately 15 min to train on one NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU.
source: The CNN took approximately 15 min to train on one NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, which amounts to 60 CPU hours for an equivalent CPU-only training procedure.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of the method.

claim: Visual inspection of the haplotypes or genotypes of the top candidate regions remains a necessary criterion to accurately assess whether a region may have been under adaptive introgression.
source: We note, however, that, as with previous methods, visual inspection of the haplotypes or genotypes of the top candidate regions remains a necessary criterion to accurately assess whether a region may have been under adaptive introgression.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the analysis of candidate regions.

claim: The performance of the method necessarily depends upon the demographic history of the populations involved.
source: The performance of our method necessarily depends upon the demographic history of the populations involved.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of performance under different demographic models.

claim: It is more challenging to detect AI when the timing of gene flow is younger or the introgressing population is more diverged from the panel that is used to represent it.
source: We found it more challenging to detect AI when the timing of gene flow is younger or the introgressing population is more diverged from the panel that is used to represent it.
evidence: This is based on the comparison of performance for different demographic scenarios.

claim: For the two putative pulses of Denisovan gene flow, the model has greater recall with AI for the more ancient pulse (94% versus 83.6%).
source: Furthermore, for the two putative pulses of Denisovan gene flow (Jacobs et al., 2019), we find our model has greater recall with AI for the more ancient pulse (94% versus 83.6%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), likely because haplotypes from the older pulse have more time to rise in frequency.
evidence: This is supported by the performance evaluation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Recall is diminished when the onset of selection is more recent.
source: Similarly, recall is diminished when the onset of selection is more recent.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of CNN predictions across different parameter values.

claim: Distinguishing AI from a selective sweep is relatively easier than distinguishing AI from neutral variation.
source: We also found that distinguishing AI from a selective sweep (hard or soft), is relatively easier than distinguishing AI from neutral variation.
evidence: This is based on the confusion matrix and performance analysis.

claim: The method requires sequencing data from the population from which the introgression event originated.
source: Our method requires sequencing data from the population from which the introgression event originated.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements of the method.

claim: The method can take either phased or unphased data as input.
source: The method can take either phased or unphased data as input.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: The method requires called genotypes and is therefore not yet suitable for genomes sequenced at low coverage.
source: It does, however, require called genotypes and is therefore not yet suitable for genomes sequenced at low coverage.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the method.

claim: CNNs are a powerful approach to detecting adaptive introgression and can recover both known and novel selection candidates that were introduced via admixture.
source: In summary, we have shown that CNNs are a powerful approach to detecting adaptive introgression and can recover both known and novel selection candidates that were introduced via admixture.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the results of the study.

claim: Deep learning can serve as a very powerful tool for population genetic inference.
source: As in previous applications to other problems in the field (Sheehan and Song, 2016; Flagel et al., 2019; Schrider and Kern, 2018; Villanea and Schraiber, 2019; Mondal et al., 2019; Torada et al., 2019; Isildak et al., 2021), this exemplifies how deep learning can serve as a very powerful tool for population genetic inference.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: For CNN training, simulations were performed under three scenarios: neutral mutations only; positive selection of a de novo mutation in the recipient population (selective sweep); and positive selection of a derived mutation that was transferred via gene flow from the donor population to the recipient population (adaptive introgression, AI).
source: For CNN training, we performed simulations under three scenarios: neutral mutations only; positive selection of a de novo mutation in the recipient population (selective sweep); and positive selection of a derived mutation that was transferred via gene flow from the donor population to the recipient population (adaptive introgression, AI).
evidence: This describes the simulation procedure used for training the CNN.

claim: In the sweep and AI scenarios, the selection coefficient was drawn log-uniformly from between 0.0001 and 0.1 for Europeans.
source: In the sweep and AI scenarios, the selection coefficient was drawn log-uniformly from between 0.0001 and 0.1 for Europeans and between 0.001 and 0.1 for Melanesians (in the latter case, very few selected alleles survive with a very small selection coefficient, so we narrowed the range to reduce computational burden).
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters used for training the CNN.

claim: A rejection-sampling approach was used to condition on the selected allele's frequency being ≥5% in the recipient population at the end of the simulation.
source: For both the sweep scenario and the AI scenario, we used a rejection-sampling approach to condition on the selected allele's frequency being ≥ in the recipient population at the end of the simulation.
evidence: This describes the simulation procedure used for training the CNN.

claim: Major alleles (those with sample frequency greater than 0.5 after merging all individuals) were encoded in the matrix as 0, while minor alleles were encoded as 1.
source: Major alleles (those with sample frequency greater than 0.5 after merging all individuals) were encoded in the matrix as 0, while minor alleles were encoded as 1.
evidence: This describes the data encoding procedure for the CNN.

claim: Only sites with a minor allele frequency >5% were retained.
source: Only sites with a minor allele frequency >5% were retained.
evidence: This describes the data filtering procedure for the CNN.

claim: For sweep and AI simulations, the site of the selected mutation was excluded.
source: For sweep and AI simulations, we excluded the site of the selected mutation.
evidence: This describes the data filtering procedure for the CNN.

claim: The resized haplotypes/individuals within each submatrix were ordered left-to-right by decreasing similarity to the donor population.
source: The resized haplotypes/individuals within each submatrix were ordered left-to-right by decreasing similarity to the donor population, calculated as the Euclidean distance to the average minor-allele density of the donor population (analogous to a vector of the donor allele frequencies).
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure for the CNN.

claim: The CNN model was implemented in Keras, configured to use the Tensorflow backend.
source: We implemented the CNN model in Keras (Chollet, 2015), configured to use the Tensorflow backend (Abadi et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the implementation of the CNN.

claim: The first layer of the network is a batch normalisation layer.
source: We instead made the first layer of our network a batch normalisation layer, which simultaneously converts the input layer to floating point numbers and learns the best normalisation of the data for the network.
evidence: This describes the architecture of the CNN.

claim: Pooling layers are not included in the CNN architecture; instead a 2 × 2 stride size is used to reduce the output size of successive blocks.
source: We do not include pooling layers, as is common in a CNN architecture (e.g. Torada et al., 2019), and instead use a 2 × 2 stride size to reduce the output size of successive blocks (Springenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the architecture of the CNN.

claim: 100,000 independent simulations for each of the three selection scenarios were partitioned into training and validation sets (approximate 90%/10% split).
source: We partitioned 100,000 independent simulations for each of the three selection scenarios into training and validation sets (approximate 90%/10% split).
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the CNN.

claim: The model was trained for three epochs, with model weights updated after batches of 64, using the Adam optimiser and cross-entropy for the loss function.
source: The model was trained for three epochs, with model weights updated after batches of 64, using the Adam optimiser and cross-entropy for the loss function.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the CNN.

claim: Three calibration methods were tested: beta regression, isotonic regression, and Platt scaling.
source: We tested three calibration methods: beta regression (Kull et al., 2017), isotonic regression (Chakravarti, 1989), and Platt, 1999 scaling.
evidence: This describes the calibration procedure for the CNN.

claim: Both beta calibration and isotonic regression gave well-calibrated probabilities compared with uncalibrated model outputs.
source: Both beta calibration and isotonic regression gave well-calibrated probabilities compared with uncalibrated model outputs, and for our predictions on empirical data we chose to apply beta calibration due to its relative simplicity.
evidence: This is supported by the calibration analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplements.

claim: Beta calibration was chosen for predictions on empirical data due to its relative simplicity.
source: Both beta calibration and isotonic regression gave well-calibrated probabilities compared with uncalibrated model outputs, and for our predictions on empirical data we chose to apply beta calibration due to its relative simplicity.
evidence: This describes the calibration procedure applied to empirical data.

claim: Average saliency maps were computed by averaging over a set of input-specific saliency maps that were calculated for a set of 300 simulated genotype matrices for each simulated scenario.
source: We computed average saliency maps, by averaging over a set of input-specific saliency maps that were calculated for a set of 300 simulated genotype matrices for each simulated scenario.
evidence: This describes the procedure for computing saliency maps.

claim: The input-specific saliency maps were calculated using tf-keras-vis v0.5.5 configured to use 'vanilla' saliency maps.
source: The input-specific saliency maps were calculated using tf-keras-vis v0.5.5 (Kubota, 2020) configured to use 'vanilla' saliency maps.
evidence: This describes the procedure for computing saliency maps.

claim: Manhattan plots show each data point as a 100 kbp window that moves along the genome in steps of size 20 kbp.
source: We show Manhattan plots where each data point is a 100 kbp window that moves along the genome in steps of size 20 kbp.
evidence: This describes the visualization of results on empirical data.

claim: Gene annotations were extracted from the Ensembl release 87 GFF3 file.
source: Gene annotations were extracted from the Ensembl release 87 GFF3 file (with GRCh37/hg19 coordinates), obtained via ensembl's ftp server.
evidence: This describes the data sources used for gene annotation.

claim: Genes which intersected with the 30 top ranking CNN predictions or a 100 kbp flanking region were reported.
source: We extracted the columns with source='ensembl_havana' and type='gene', and report the genes which intersected with the 30 top ranking CNN predictions or a 100 kbp flanking region.
evidence: This describes the procedure for identifying candidate genes.
